svg.title: Intravesical BCG: the shape of a course, the side-effect timeline, and the signals that mean going back the same day
svg.desc: Schematic in three panels. The first, "the shape of a course: six weeks is only the beginning", draws a timeline: a six-week induction, one instillation a week, then maintenance with three weekly instillations again at 3, 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 and 36 months, up to 27 in all; a note says the length of a course is not a score, and that who is given BCG and how often is decided by risk stratification. Below the timeline are two evidence cards. SWOG 8507 is a randomised trial: 660 patients had the six-week induction, 550 were randomised at three months to maintenance or none, and the primary analysis set was the 384 patients disease-free at randomisation; median recurrence-free survival was 35.7 months without maintenance against 76.8 months with it, p less than 0.0001; median worsening-free survival 111.5 months against not reached; five-year overall survival 78% against 83%. The card records that the authors themselves noted patients with bad side effects simply stopped maintenance, so the trial could not see severe toxicity. The second card is EORTC 30962, a randomised 2x2 trial (one-third dose or full dose, by one year or three years) in intermediate- and high-risk Ta and T1 disease, 1,355 patients in the intention-to-treat set, median follow-up 7.1 years: in high-risk patients two extra years reduced recurrence (hazard ratio 1.61, 95% confidence interval 1.13 to 2.30, p=0.009) but only at full dose; at intermediate risk two extra years at full dose bought nothing; progression and survival did not differ across the four arms. The second panel, "the days after an instillation, and how many people get through the course", shows a three-step timeline: bladder irritation begins 4 to 6 hours after instillation, lasts 24 to 72 hours, and is usually only marked after the third instillation; about 60% of patients get bladder irritation. The adverse-event table in the label, 674 patients including 153 with carcinoma in situ: painful urination 60% (grade 3 or worse 11%), urinary frequency 40% (7%), flu-like syndrome 33% (9%), fever 20% (8%). Completion: the guideline states more than half of patients cannot complete one year of maintenance, and in the three-year maintenance arm of EORTC 30962 only 34% completed the whole course. The same panel lists three things often mistaken for a contraindication which are not - white cells on the urine dipstick, invisible haematuria, asymptomatic bacteriuria - and the group that really has to wait, quoting the label verbatim: "Treatment should be postponed for at least 1 week following transurethral resection, biopsy, traumatic catheterization, or gross hematuria"; the guideline advises at least two weeks after a resection, and the contraindications section separately lists immunosuppression and active tuberculosis. The third panel is a red box, "what means going back the same day, rather than waiting for the next visit", listing verbatim the four signals the label calls suggestive of systemic BCG infection: flu-like fever lasting more than 72 hours; a fever reaching 103°F (about 39.4°C), or a temperature of 38.5°C (101.3°F) or above lasting more than two to three days; systemic symptoms getting worse with each instillation, or persistently abnormal liver blood tests; local acute inflammation - prostatitis, epididymitis, orchitis - lasting more than two to three days. Above the red box the label is quoted: "Deaths have been reported as a result of systemic BCG infection and sepsis.", together with the label's other sentence that malaise, fever and chills lasting one to two days usually reflect a hypersensitivity reaction. Below it: there is only one thing for you to do - go back the same day and say clearly which day the last instillation was; stopping the drug, cultures, imaging and referral are the clinical side, and the guideline's threshold is a persistent fever above 38.5°C for more than 48 hours, at which point BCG is stopped permanently. Three rates close the panel: serious side effects in fewer than 5% of patients, systemic BCG infection 1% to 2%, and among 5,033 exposed people in the Swedish national database a five-year cumulative notified tuberculosis diagnosis rate of 1.1%. The figure ends by stating that it is not a tool for deciding whether your own case is serious enough; that judgement belongs to the person who can see your results.

g.text: BCG INTRAVESICAL - COURSE, SIDE EFFECTS, RED FLAGS
The shape of a BCG course, the days after an instillation,
and what means going back the same day
This figure does three things: it shows how long one round of BCG actually is, what the body does in the days after an instillation, and
which signals mean going back the same day rather than waiting for the next booked clinic.
Every cell carries its source and who the patients were. The cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the data
points must not be compared directly.
The lines in the red panel are the label's own wording, not thresholds I assembled; the same section of the label reads "Deaths have been reported as a
result of systemic BCG infection and sepsis."
The shape of a course: six weeks is only the beginning
The full schedule as the guideline describes it: a six-week induction, one instillation a week; then maintenance, three weekly instillations again at 3, 6, 12, 18, 24,
30 and 36 months, up to 27 in all.
Induction
six weeks, once a week
month 3
month 6
month 12
month 18
month 24
month 30
month 36
Maintenance
three weeks each time
up to 27 in all
The length of a course is not a score. It is what risk group, tolerance and drug supply settle on together - and who is given BCG, and how often, is decided by risk
stratification.
Does maintenance do anything
SWOG 8507
design
randomised trial
population
recurrent Ta, T1 and carcinoma in situ; 660 patients had the six-week induction, 550
were randomised at three months to maintenance or none
primary analysis set
the 384 patients who were disease-free at randomisation
result
median recurrence-free survival 35.7 months (no maintenance) against 76.8 months
(maintenance), p less than 0.0001; median worsening-free survival 111.5 months
against not reached; five-year overall survival 78% against 83%
The authors note it themselves: patients with bad side effects simply stopped
maintenance, so the trial could not see severe toxicity.
And for how long
EORTC 30962
design
randomised trial, 2x2 design (one-third dose or full dose, by one year or three years)
population
intermediate- and high-risk Ta and T1; 1,355 patients in the intention-to-treat set
follow-up
median 7.1 years
result
in high-risk patients two extra years reduced recurrence (hazard ratio 1.61, 95%
confidence interval 1.13 to 2.30, p=0.009), but only at full dose; at intermediate risk
two extra years at full dose bought nothing
Progression and survival did not differ across the four arms. The two extra
years buy fewer recurrences, not fewer deaths.
The days after an instillation, and how many people get through the course
The label is specific: about 60% of patients get bladder irritation. Each one being harder than the last is what this drug does; it is not you getting weaker.
4 to 6 hours after instillation
bladder irritation begins
lasting 24 to 72 hours
it usually settles inside this window
after the third instillation
the label: usually only marked from here on
The adverse-event table in the label, 674 patients (153 of them with
carcinoma in situ)
In brackets: the proportion that was grade 3 or worse.
painful urination
grade 3 or worse 11%
urinary frequency
grade 3 or worse 7%
flu-like syndrome
grade 3 or worse 9%
fever
grade 3 or worse 8%
How many get through it
The guideline: more than half of patients cannot complete one year of
maintenance.
In the three-year maintenance arm of EORTC 30962, only 34% completed the
whole course.
Three things often mistaken for a contraindication, which are not
white cells on the urine dipstick
invisible (microscopic) haematuria
asymptomatic bacteriuria
None of the three calls for preventive antibiotics, and a positive tuberculin skin test is
not a reason to be excluded either.
This is the group that really has to wait
Treatment should be postponed for at least 1 week following transurethral resection, biopsy, traumatic catheterization, or gross hematuria
The label: instilling while the lining is bleeding may promote systemic infection, so after a resection, a biopsy, a traumatic catheterisation or visible blood in the urine
there has to be at least a week in between; the guideline advises at least two weeks after a resection. The contraindications section separately lists immunosuppression
and active tuberculosis.
What means going back the same day, rather than waiting for the next visit
"Fever is a normal reaction" cannot stand as one sentence; it has to be split in two. The label: malaise, fever and chills lasting one to two days usually reflect a
hypersensitivity reaction. But the four below are what the label calls suggestive of systemic BCG infection, which may need antituberculous treatment.
flu-like fever lasting more than 72 hours
a fever reaching 103°F (about 39.4°C), or a temperature of 38.5°C
(101.3°F) or above lasting more than two to three days
systemic symptoms getting worse with each instillation, or
persistently abnormal liver blood tests
local acute inflammation - prostatitis, epididymitis, orchitis - lasting
more than two to three days
There is only one thing for you to do: go back the same day, and say clearly which day the last instillation was.
Stopping the drug, cultures, imaging and referral are the clinical side of it - the guideline's threshold is a persistent fever above 38.5°C for more than 48 hours, at which
point BCG is stopped permanently and urine culture, blood tests, a chest X-ray and an infectious-diseases opinion are arranged straight away.
The rates belong in the same panel, not hidden elsewhere
serious side effects
fewer than 5% of patients, and nearly all can be
managed effectively
systemic BCG infection
5,033 exposed people in the Swedish national
database
five-year cumulative notified tuberculosis diagnosis
This figure is not a tool for deciding "is mine serious enough". The signals are there so you telephone and come in the same day; how serious it is, is judged by the
person who can see your results.
Schematic, redrawn from the TICE BCG US prescribing information (revised 2/2026), the EAU guidelines on non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer (2026 edition), SWOG 8507
(Lamm 2000) and EORTC 30962 (Oddens 2013); not reproduced from their figures. The cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the data points must
not be compared directly.
